extracted.intended_audience: postdoctoral researchers applying for Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA) Postdoctoral Fellowships (European or Global)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, evaluative guidance for preparing and submitting a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Postdoctoral Fellowship (European or Global) proposal, covering eligibility, host/supervisor selection, proposal writing, and the official evaluation criteria and process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobility eligibility (12/36 rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: You must not have resided or carried out your main activity in the country of the host institution for more than 12 months in the 36 months immediately preceding the call deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 36-month window is counted backward from the exact deadline date (not from planned start). Count is cumulative (separate short stays add up). Remote work counts for both the country of physical residence AND the employer's country. What doesn't count: short vacations, conference attendance, brief research visits where home institution remained main employer, compulsory national/military service, time in refugee status procedures. Be precise about exceptions—'brief research visits' excludes extended secondments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fellowship type eligibility: European vs Global
rubrics_metrics.description: Different rules apply depending on whether you apply for a European Fellowship (EF) or a Global Fellowship (GF).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: European Fellowships: open to researchers of any nationality; host must be in EU Member State or Horizon Europe Associated Country; duration 12–24 months. Global Fellowships: require EU/Associated Country nationality or 5+ years continuous residence in Europe; include an outgoing phase (12–24 months) at a third-country host plus a mandatory 12-month return phase to Europe; total 24–36 months. For GF, the mobility rule applies to the third-country outgoing host, not the European return host.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit-cost funding model and monthly allowances
rubrics_metrics.description: MSCA-PF uses standardized unit costs (monthly rates) paid to the host institution, not reimbursement of actual itemized costs by the researcher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical monthly amounts (Work Programme 2024–2025): Living Allowance €5,990 (adjusted by country coefficient), Mobility Allowance €710, Family Allowance €660 (if applicable), Research/Training Costs €1,000 (to host), Management/Indirect Costs €650 (to host). Country correction coefficients modify living allowance (~80% to >160%). Fellows are employees of the host institution under a full employment contract with social security; host is the legal beneficiary and receives funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Career Development Plan (mandatory deliverable)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Career Development Plan must be produced (mandatory deliverable) within six months of project start.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Career Development Plan is evaluated as part of the training and two-way knowledge transfer assessment—be concrete about courses, mentoring, secondments, and career milestones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way knowledge transfer requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals must demonstrate two-way knowledge transfer: what the researcher will gain from the host AND what the researcher will contribute to the host.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators specifically assess both directions. Proposals that only describe benefits flowing to the researcher score poorly. For every listed training benefit, justify what you bring that the host doesn’t already have; explain unique expertise, methodological innovations, or international connections you contribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondments: strategic justification and rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondments are temporary stays at another organization during the fellowship and are allowed under specific rules and only if justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For European Fellowships, secondments may total up to one-third of fellowship duration. For Global Fellowships, secondments may occur only during the outgoing phase (not during the mandatory return phase). Include secondments only when clearly justified (e.g., unique equipment or skills). Unjustified secondments raise red flags. Technical note: secondment hosts should NOT be encoded as Associated Partners—only non-academic placement host (NAP) and the third-country outgoing host (for GF) are Associated Partners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation structure: three weighted criteria and scoring rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals are scored on Excellence (50%), Impact (30%), and Implementation (20%). Each criterion is assessed on a 0–5 scale with half-point increments; each criterion has a threshold of 3.0/5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing any single criterion (below 3) means rejection. Typical funding cut-offs are very high (often 90–95% total weighted score), so merely passing thresholds is insufficient for success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence — Quality and pertinence of objectives (1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectives should be ambitious, measurable, and verifiable, and clearly go beyond the current state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define 3–5 clear, measurable objectives and link each explicitly to work packages and verifiable outputs. Avoid vague objectives such as 'explore'—prefer outcomes like 'develop and validate a novel method for X, benchmarking against Y and Z.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence — Soundness of methodology (1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The approach must be feasible and appropriate, incorporate interdisciplinary methods where relevant, address the gender dimension where applicable, and follow open science practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include methodological details adequate to judge feasibility; describe interdisciplinary integration and data/analysis practices. Where relevant, state open science plans (data sharing, pre-registration, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence — Quality of supervision, training, and two-way transfer (1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supervision and training plans must be high quality: supervisor qualifications, a concrete training plan, and clear two-way knowledge transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate supervisor’s mentoring experience and relevant track record (MSCA/ERC experience strengthens perceived feasibility). Make training activities specific (who teaches what, by which methods, when) and tie them to career outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence — Quality of researcher's professional experience (1.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: The researcher must have the track record and competencies to deliver the project and bring unique strengths to the host.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a concise CV emphasizing relevant competencies, prior achievements, and evidence of independence or key contributions. Explain why you (the researcher) are the right person for this specific project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact — Career perspectives and employability (2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal must explain how the fellowship will concretely advance the researcher's career and employability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific next-step positions, target institutions, or practical career milestones enabled by the fellowship. Generic claims about 'enhancing career prospects' are flagged as weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact — Dissemination, exploitation, and communication (2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be specific, measurable plans for dissemination to scientific communities, exploitation into applications, and communication to broader audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe targeted journals/conferences, IP/translation strategies, stakeholder engagement, and measurable outreach activities. Vague statements about 'publishing in high-impact journals' are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact — Contribution to expected impacts (2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the broader scientific, societal, and economic contributions and why they matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the link between project outputs and expected impacts explicit and evidence-based; avoid generic high-level statements without concrete pathways to impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation — Work plan quality (3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The timeline and work plan must be realistic, include appropriate milestones and deliverables, and identify risks with mitigation strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a Gantt chart to visualize work packages, deliverables, and milestones. Avoid clustering deliverables only at project end—distribute outputs logically across the timeline. Explicitly list risks and realistic mitigation measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation — Host institution capacity and supervision arrangements (3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The host must have appropriate infrastructure, resources, and supervision arrangements to support the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document access to facilities and equipment, institutional support offices, and supervisory commitment. Host institutional characteristics (HR Excellence in Research, dedicated MSCA support office) strengthen Implementation scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict Part B1 page limit and proposal format
rubrics_metrics.description: Part B1 (the core technical proposal) has a strict 10-page limit; content beyond page 10 will be invisible to evaluators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere exactly to the PDF and formatting requirements. Part A contains administrative online forms; Part B is the uploaded PDF. Plan content density and prioritization accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear, measurable objectives linked to work packages
rubrics_metrics.description: Define 3–5 clear, measurable objectives and link each explicitly to a work package and verifiable outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objectives should be measurable and verifiable (milestones, deliverables, performance indicators). Each objective must map to concrete tasks and outputs visible in the Gantt and deliverables table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of training activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Training descriptions must be concrete: which techniques, from whom, through what activities, and when in the timeline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generic statements like 'acquiring new skills' fail. Spell out courses, workshops, mentoring sessions, secondments, and how these translate to career outcomes and competencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compelling opening and narrative structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Open the proposal with a concise, compelling statement of novelty, importance, and fit between researcher and host.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first paragraph should state what's new, why it matters, and why you're the right person—don't bury significance. Evaluators read many proposals; a strong opening improves engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid common pitfalls and anti-patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and avoid common weaknesses that lower scores across criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent problems include: weak knowledge transfer narratives, vague training plans, generic career statements, deliverables clustered at project end, unjustified secondments, and technical encoding errors (wrong fellowship type, secondment hosts listed as Associated Partners, inconsistencies between Part A and Part B). Address these proactively during drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical and administrative accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative details must be correct and consistent across submission materials to avoid eligibility/administrative problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common encoding errors: wrong fellowship type selection, listing secondment hosts as Associated Partners, inconsistencies between Part A and Part B. Ensure accurate host/partner coding and internal institutional sign-offs; many hosts impose internal deadlines to ensure administrative quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervisor and host selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose hosts and supervisors based on research complementarity, supervisory experience, and institutional support—not merely prestige.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer hosts with complementary (not overlapping) expertise so clear two-way transfer exists. Supervisors with MSCA/ERC experience and strong mentoring records improve feasibility perception. Institutions with dedicated MSCA support offices, HR Excellence in Research certification, and clear access to equipment/facilities are advantageous. Watch for red flags: slow communication, absent supervisor during fellowship, unwillingness to engage in proposal development, or overlapping expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Researcher outreach timeline and email contents
rubrics_metrics.description: Start contact with potential supervisors well before the deadline and structure initial outreach effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial contact should occur 6–9 months before the deadline (9–12 months preferred). An effective first email includes: brief personal introduction (2–3 sentences), clear MSCA eligibility statement, intended evaluation panel, concise CV (≤5 pages), brief motivation (half page), and a one-page project sketch showing synergies and mutual benefits. Visiting the host is ideal; video calls are acceptable alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resubmission and eligibility reset rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Resubmission rules govern whether a previous proposal can be resubmitted and how host changes affect eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals scoring below 70% with the same researcher-host combination cannot be resubmitted the following year. Proposals above 70% may resubmit; evaluators may access the previous year's ESR. Changing host institution resets eligibility regardless of prior score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation process and feedback (ESR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligible proposals undergo eligibility checks and are evaluated by at least three independent experts; consensus is reached in panel discussions and applicants receive an Evaluation Summary Report (ESR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals are ranked by total weighted score within each disciplinary panel. The ESR provides criterion-level feedback useful for resubmission or alternative funding routes (e.g., Seal of Excellence). Understanding the evaluation mechanics helps interpret feedback and subsequent strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic timeline for proposal development
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested timeline and milestones from initial contact to final submission to ensure thorough preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested milestones: 12 months — identify hosts and start outreach; 9–6 months — confirm supervisor and develop concept; 6–4 months — draft proposal sections and coordinate with institutional research office; 4–2 months — multiple draft iterations and gather feedback; 1 month — final revisions, ethics completion, institutional sign-off; 2 weeks — final polish and technical submission checks. Many institutions enforce internal deadlines 1–3 weeks before the EU deadline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic positioning vs prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: Research complementarity matters more than host prestige for scoring two-way transfer and feasibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposing to join a group already expert in your exact methods suggests limited contribution and weak two-way transfer. Emphasize what you will learn and how your expertise complements the host's capabilities rather than duplicating them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remote-work residency counting rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Remote work counts toward residency in both the country of physical residence and the employer's country for mobility eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of COVID-era remote arrangements; they may create ineligibility for multiple host countries. Carefully calculate any remote employment periods in the 36-month window.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding/host practicalities and employment rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The host institution is the legal beneficiary; the fellow is an employee under local labor law, with social security coverage and contractual employment rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand employment conditions (salary adjustments via country coefficients), access to facilities, pension/health insurance implications, and how host institutions implement contracts. Supervisor and institutional HR engagement are critical for smooth post-award implementation.
